newsitem.title: GERMANY: German leaders discuss possible spending cuts.
newsitem.headline: German leaders discuss possible spending cuts.

text.p: Leaders of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition stressed possible spending cuts on Tuesday in talks on how best to plug gaps in Germany's 1997 budget, coalition sources said.
Another, larger group of officials started a three-day, closed-door session in Schwerin to estimate the tax shortfall.

Opposition and private sector officials have said that mainly because of high unemployment, 1997 tax shortfall could be running as much as 20 billion marks ($11.8 billion) higher than the deficit already projected in the budget.
Ten economists polled by Reuters showed average projections of a 16 billion mark shortfall.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel contested that view, but conceded that the shortfall could be eight billion marks.

Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier, deputy head of the opposition Social Democrats' parliamentary faction, repeated her call that the government draw up a supplementary budget, and "finally do something for the unemployed, so it can get a grip on its finances."
Germany, like other European nations, is under pressure to reduce its government deficit to three percent of total economic output this year, to qualify for European monetary union (EMU).
The federal budget foresees a deficit of 53.4 billion marks for 1997, in line with the EMU goal, but many observers are sceptical it can hit the mark.
Waigel has refused to exclude a spending freeze as a possible remedy, and said the government would decide appropriate measures based on the tax estimate.

Federal, state and central bank officials met with private-sector advisors in a semiannual closed-door conference in the east German town of Schwerin to hammer out hard numbers. Their results are due to be announced on Thursday.

Private research institutes see German economic growth this year at about 2.25 percent, lower than the government projection of 2.5 percent. That quarter-point difference alone could mean two billion marks in tax revenues.
Kohl said in a television interview this week that coalition leaders would discuss possible spending cuts and tax increases to stop the budget gap at today's talks.
"Then that will be discussed, and in all directions," Kohl said.

Peter Hintze, general secretary of Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU), declined to disclose details, but said there had been a "critical development", as tax revenues were declining despite an upturn in the economy.
This underscores the need for a comprehensive reform of the tax system, as proposed by Waigel, he said.
The coalition leaders will also discuss pension reform and continued aid to east Germany, but would not hold a news conference on Tuesday as originally scheduled.
